title.en: Pericardial effusion: fluid around the heart

idea.en: Spot pericardial fluid in subcostal and parasternal views and separate it from pleural fluid.

steps.en: What you see: A dark echo free space surrounds the heart and persists through systole and diastole. Small effusions sit behind the left ventricle only. Larger ones wrap around the whole heart and the heart swings inside the fluid. A large fluid collection with a swinging heart may show electrical alternans on the ECG. Right atrial collapse in late diastole warns that pressure in the sac is rising.

Normal values with units: Pericardial separation. Normally no persistent echo free space. Small below 10 mm and usually posterior only. Moderate 10 to 20 mm around the heart. Large above 20 mm, usually with a swinging heart.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on the pericardium

Inferior vena cava. Normal diameter 21 mm or below with collapse of 50 percent or more on a sniff. A dilated cava with minimal collapse suggests raised right atrial pressure.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on the inferior vena cava

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low QRS voltage when fluid is large. A swinging heart gives electrical alternans where the QRS height changes from beat to beat.
ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: Heart sounds are muffled when fluid is large. A pericardial friction rub points to inflammatory disease and is best heard with the patient leaning forward.

spot.en: Landmarks: Bright pericardial line bounding the fluid outside
Echo free space around the ventricles
Descending aorta behind the left atrium in long axis
Right atrium and right ventricle for collapse signs
What to report: Largest fluid separation in millimetres with its position around the heart
Any chamber collapse with its timing in the cardiac cycle
Inferior vena cava size and collapse
Likely cause clues such as fibrin strands, clot or a dilated aorta
Red flags needing urgent referral: Any right ventricular diastolic collapse with tachycardia or hypotension, needs urgent drainage assessment
Large effusion above 20 mm with a swinging heart, needs urgent cardiology review
Effusion after chest trauma or a cardiac procedure, needs immediate senior review
Pitfalls: A small posterior space in early systole can be normal fat, so require persistence through the cycle.
Loculated effusions after surgery hide in one recess, so scan every window before ruling out fluid.
Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis, so never delay drainage for more images when the patient is unstable.
Figure: Parasternal long axis separates a posterior effusion from the descending aorta, which lies behind the left atrium. View tte_plax

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Start subcostal with the patient supine and knees bent, pressing gently below the xiphisternum.
Aim toward the left shoulder and fan until all four chambers and the pericardial sac appear.
Confirm the fluid lies inside the bright pericardial line and not in the pleural space.
Move to the parasternal long axis and check behind the left ventricle and beside the right ventricle.
Measure the largest echo free space at end diastole in millimetres.

Common mistakes and how to correct them: Calling left pleural fluid a pericardial effusion. Fix: Use position relative to the descending aorta. Fluid in front of the aorta is pericardial, fluid behind the aorta is pleural.
Calling epicardial fat an effusion. Fix: Reduce gain and check that the space stays dark through the whole cycle. Fat moves with the wall and looks brighter.
Missing a loculated effusion by scanning one view only. Fix: Sweep through the whole heart because small effusions hide behind one wall only.

remember.en: Link low voltage and alternans on the ECG to large effusions.

why.en: Pericardial fluid lies in front of the descending aorta while pleural fluid tracks behind it.

q.en: Which separation marks a large effusion?

why.en: Large means above 20 mm of echo free space, usually with a swinging heart.

q.en: The right ventricle collapses in diastole and the patient is hypotensive. What next?

o.en: Urgent drainage assessment with senior help
Routine echo follow up in one year

why.en: Diastolic chamber collapse with hypotension is tamponade physiology and needs urgent drainage.
